target: Silakan duduk, Pak Budi datang sebentar lagi.
english: Please have a seat, Mr. Budi is coming shortly.
tip: silakan invites someone to do something for their own benefit: Silakan duduk = please have a seat. tolong is the other 'please' – it asks someone to help you.

target: Jangan pergi sekarang, makanannya belum datang.
english: Don't go now, the food hasn't arrived yet.
tip: Commands are negated with jangan, not tidak: jangan pergi = don't go. tidak only states facts (dia tidak pergi = he doesn't go) – it can't forbid anything.

target: Jangan makan terlalu cepat, nanti sakit perut.
english: Don't eat too fast, you will get a stomachache.
tip: nanti in a warning means 'or else': nanti sakit perut = you'll get a stomachache.

target: Boleh saya pinjam pulpen kamu sebentar?
english: May I borrow your pen for a moment?
tip: Boleh saya pinjam? asks permission (may I). bisa is ability (can): saya bisa berenang = I can swim. English 'can' covers both jobs; Indonesian splits them.

target: Coba tanya ke petugas di depan sana.
english: Try asking the attendant over there at the front.
tip: coba before a verb softens a suggestion: coba tanya = try asking.

target: Mari kita mulai rapat ini sekarang.
english: Let's start this meeting now.
tip: mari kita + verb = 'let's': mari kita mulai = let's begin. mari is the polite version – among friends you'll hear ayo instead: Ayo mulai!

target: Mari kita berfoto bersama di pantai.
english: Let's take a photo together at the beach.
tip: ber- turns a noun into 'do X': berfoto = take a photo.

target: Silakan telepon saya kalau ada masalah.
english: Please call me if there is a problem.
tip: kalau = if/when in everyday speech: kalau ada masalah = if there is a problem.

target: Kemarin saya pergi ke pasar dengan ibu saya.
english: Yesterday I went to the market with my mother.
tip: Time words do the past-tense work: Kemarin saya pergi. = Yesterday I went. The verb never changes.

target: Tadi pagi saya bangun jam enam.
english: This morning I woke up at six.
tip: tadi = earlier today: tadi pagi = this morning (already past).

target: Waktu saya kecil, keluarga kami tinggal di desa.
english: When I was little, our family lived in a village.
tip: waktu opens a past when-clause: Waktu saya kecil... = When I was little...

target: Bulan lalu saya mulai belajar bahasa Indonesia.
english: Last month I started learning Indonesian.
tip: lalu after a time word = last: bulan lalu = last month, minggu lalu = last week.

target: Tadi saya minum kopi, terus lupa membayar.
english: Earlier I drank coffee, and then forgot to pay.
tip: terus strings actions in speech: ..., terus lupa = ..., and then (I) forgot.

target: Waktu kami tiba, toko itu sudah tutup.
english: When we arrived, the shop was already closed.
tip: tutup never changes for tense – sudah alone tells you the shop 'was already closed': sudah tutup. Time in Indonesian lives in the markers, not in verb endings.

target: Dua hari lalu kami berenang di pantai.
english: Two days ago we swam at the beach.
tip: lalu after a time span = ago: dua hari lalu = two days ago.

target: Saya membeli tiket dulu, kemudian menunggu di peron.
english: I bought a ticket first, then waited on the platform.
tip: dulu after a verb means first, not long ago: membeli tiket dulu = buy a ticket first. At the start of a sentence, dulu means back in the day.

target: Kemarin malam listrik mati selama dua jam.
english: Last night the electricity was out for two hours.
tip: Duration 'for' is selama, not untuk: mati selama dua jam = out for two hours. untuk is 'for' as purpose or recipient (untuk kamu = for you).

target: Saya sakit kepala sejak tadi pagi.
english: I have had a headache since this morning.
tip: sakit + body part = it hurts: sakit kepala = headache, sakit perut = stomachache.

target: Anak saya demam sejak kemarin malam.
english: My child has had a fever since last night.
tip: English needs 'has had a fever since' – Indonesian states it flat: demam sejak kemarin malam, no tense change. Sejak alone signals it started then and still holds.

target: Saya mau minum obat dulu sebelum tidur.
english: I want to take my medicine first before sleeping.
tip: You drink medicine in Indonesian, even pills: minum obat is literally 'drink medicine'. There's no separate 'take' verb for it.

target: Badan saya capek setelah kerja seminggu penuh.
english: My body is worn out after a full week of work.
tip: capek is the everyday spoken 'tired': Badan saya capek. The formal counterpart is lelah – same meaning, but capek is what you'll actually hear in conversation.

target: Dokter bilang saya harus istirahat tiga hari.
english: The doctor said I have to rest for three days.
tip: bilang is the conversational 'say': Dokter bilang saya harus istirahat = the doctor said. Formal writing prefers berkata or mengatakan – bilang is for speech.

target: Ayah pergi ke rumah sakit untuk periksa kesehatan.
english: Dad went to the hospital for a health check-up.
tip: ke-...-an builds nouns: sehat (healthy) becomes kesehatan (health).

target: Saya batuk terus sejak dua hari lalu.
english: I have been coughing constantly since two days ago.
tip: terus after a verb = keeps on: batuk terus = keeps coughing.

target: Anak itu menangis karena giginya sakit.
english: That child is crying because his tooth hurts.
tip: -nya stuck on a noun means his or her: giginya = his tooth (gigi + -nya). No separate word for 'his' – the owner hangs off the end of the noun.

target: Dia dirawat di rumah sakit selama tiga hari.
english: He was treated in the hospital for three days.
tip: Rumah sakit, literally 'sick house', is the word for hospital. Indonesian compounds put the main noun first – rumah (house) is the thing, sakit just describes it.

target: Obat ini harus diminum setelah makan.
english: This medicine must be taken after eating.
tip: di- flips the verb passive: diminum = is taken (drunk).

target: Hari ini cuacanya cerah sekali.
english: The weather today is really clear.
tip: The -nya on cuacanya isn't 'its' here – it marks the weather as the known topic, like English 'the': cuacanya cerah = the weather is clear.

target: Kalau hujan, saya naik taksi ke kantor.
english: If it rains, I take a taxi to the office.
tip: kalau starts an if-clause; no 'then' word needed after the comma: Kalau hujan, saya naik taksi.

target: Di luar sedang hujan deras.
english: It is raining heavily outside.
tip: Indonesian skips the 'it' in 'it's raining' – hujan is a verb on its own. Sedang marks in progress: sedang hujan deras = raining hard right now.
